result.content:
## Local component accessibility reports

`vp run audit:components` is an explicit, uncached audit task, separate from `ready`. It uses the
catalog-backed automatica11y development dependency, current local package builds, and authored
component examples. It doesn't send examples to a remote audit service.

The tool requires Chrome or Chromium. Check setup with
`vp exec -F @pantoken/components automatica11y doctor`. If a browser is missing, explicitly opt into
its download with `vp exec -F @pantoken/components automatica11y doctor --install-browser`.
Don't bypass an outdated-browser warning without understanding its effect on results.

Each run retains the tool's original Markdown and JSON reports and a coverage index in
`a11y-report/<run>/`. The command returns an error for infrastructure failures; accessibility
violations alone don't fail it. Keep axe and IBM findings separate, and read incomplete and
needs-review results rather than treating an empty violations list as a verdict.
The npm archetype suite retains its authored fixture mapping and local package tarballs alongside
the reports. These tarballs are test inputs, not release artifacts. Each theme/scheme case uses
the same semantic example. Keep the report's authored-fixture provenance and browser warnings.
Each npm report batch gets its own mapping; automatica11y rejects mapping entries for targets
outside that invocation.

The `component-accessibility` CI job runs this command after the build and stays outside
`ci-gate`. It's advisory even when setup or execution fails; such a failure isn't a clean audit.
The job always attempts to publish a summary and upload `component-accessibility` evidence
with 14-day retention. Download that artifact to follow the index's relative report links.
The complete matrix is browser-intensive: it runs at most two report batches at once, and CI
allows up to two hours. Original audit reports are excluded from contributor Markdown linting.
Generated pages and their assets share the `pages/` directory: automatica11y's local HTTP server
serves only the HTML file's containing directory. Verify styles over that HTTP boundary, not
only through `file://` URLs.

## The gate

- `pnpm run ready` — the pass/fail gate. It's a `vp` task DAG (`ready:all`), not a serial chain:
  `build:all` runs once, then `check:all` (`vp check`), `test:all` (`vp run -r test`), `lint:css`,
  `lint:cssdoc`, `validate:generated:only`, and `lint:markdown` fan out concurrently. Everything that reads
  generated output depends on `build:all`, so generation happens exactly once (no concurrent codegen
  race). Must pass before you're done.
- Vitest defaults to at most two workers, including coverage runs launched through the task DAG.
  This bounds test-process contention without increasing timeouts or skipping tests. For an explicit
  standalone override on a larger machine, use `vp test --maxWorkers=<count>`.

# Authoring `@pantoken/components`

`@pantoken/components` is the semantic RSCSS CSS API — a parameterized generator, not hand-written
CSS. Each documented record is one file; the bucket `index.ts` is a barrel + registry, not a monolith.

## Source layout

- `src/components/<name>/index.ts` + `<name>.css` (`COMPONENTS` registry).
- `src/components/<name>/members/<member>/index.ts` + `<member>.css` — a promoted sub-component (see
  "Sub-components (`@memberOf`)" below).
- `src/utilities/<name>/index.ts` + `<name>.css` (`UTILITIES`).
- `src/rules/{base,prose}/index.ts` + `<name>.css` (`RULES`).
- `src/declarations/<name>/index.ts` + `<name>.css` (`DECLARATIONS`).
- `src/lib/`: `helpers.ts` (ns/scope/glyph consts/spacing scales/`ComponentOptions`/`DEFAULT_PREFIX`),
  `define.ts` (`defineComponent`/`defineUtility`/`defineRule`/`defineDeclaration`), `aliases.ts`
  (`withSizeAliases`/`withAliases`), `css.ts` (the identity `css` tag), `headings.ts`,
  `field-controls.ts`.

## Sub-components (`@memberOf`)

When a component maps to a real, separately-named instui sub-component export (`Tabs.Panel`,
`Table.Row`, `Menu.Item`, …), promote it to its own record instead of documenting it as a `@part`
bullet on the parent:

- New files: `src/components/<parent>/members/<member>/<member>.css` + `index.ts`, same shape as any
  other record (`defineComponent`, registered in `COMPONENTS`, exported from `src/index.ts`).
- The record's cssdoc name is **dotted**: `@component <parent>.<member>` (e.g. `@component menu.item`)
  — this keeps member names globally unique across the whole registry even when two different parents
  have a same-named part (`menu.item` vs `side-nav-bar.item`), which a bare `item`/`item` collision
  would break for the `providers`-indexed cross-file `@memberOf`/`@structure` resolution. The TS
  identifier stays camelCase (`menuItem`/`menuItemCss`), since a dot isn't legal there anyway.
- Add `@memberOf <parent>` on the member's own record.
- **Always author an explicit `@class .<member>`** (or `@selector`) rather than relying on inference —
  a member's CSS typically keeps the parent's `@scope (.pfx-<parent>) { … }` wrapper (real cascade
  scoping, not just documentation), and inference across that boundary is unreliable; the fallback
  className for a dotted name (`.menu.item`) would also be misleading.
- **Physically move the CSS** into the member's own file — don't leave a doc-only record pointing at
  rules that still live in the parent. The aggregator just concatenates raw CSS text regardless of
  which file it came from, so this is safe even for native-element selectors with no `@scope` (e.g.
  `table.row`'s `tr`) or where a shared declaration has to be duplicated across a couple of sibling
  members (e.g. `table.-layout-stacked`'s box-reset, split per part rather than kept as one
  five-selector compound rule) — cssdoc requires each record's own file to own its own selectors.
- Remove the promoted `@part` line — a `@memberOf` record documents its own structure on its own page,
  and `@memberOf` alone (independent of nesting in the parent's own `@structure`) already feeds the
  parent's generated "Subcomponents" section.
- Give the member's own `@structure` an `@component <parent> { … }` node instead of a bare
  `@scope (.pfx-<parent>) { … }` wrapper — this embeds the member's real ancestor path (down to the
  member's own selector, with any of its own nested parts) as a cross-linked record reference, e.g.
  `@component table { tbody { tr { td {} } } }` for `table.cell`. See the `table.*` members for the
  full pattern, including a sibling-alternation node like `table.body`'s `tbody`.
- If a parent-level modifier restyles a promoted member (e.g. `tabs`'s `-variant-secondary` restyling
  `tabs.tab`, or `table`'s `-layout-stacked` restyling all six of its members), mark it inline:
  `@modifier -variant-secondary — … @affects tabs.tab — …`. Multiple `@affects <parent>.<member>`
  markers can follow one another on the same `@modifier` line.
- Register the member in `COMPONENTS` right after its parent, export `<member>Css` from `src/index.ts`
  next to the parent's export, and add it to `tests/public-surface.test.ts`'s `EXPECTED` list (that
  array is sorted before comparison, so insertion position doesn't matter). Fix any existing test that
  asserted on the parent's `xxxCss` for content that moved to the member.
- Don't promote a `@part` just because it's stylistically distinct — the bar is a **real, separately
  exported instui component** (`List.Item` yes; a passive style hook like byline's `.title`/`.description`
  or tabs' `.list`, which has no corresponding `Tabs.List` export, no).

## Alternate DOM shapes (`@variant`)

`@structure` supports `@variant <name>? { … }` blocks for a component that genuinely renders one of
several alternative DOM shapes (e.g. a `<label>` wrapping a control vs. a `<label for>` plus a sibling
control). Only add one when a second shape is **already real and CSS-supported** — check the record's
existing `@example`s and rules first; don't invent a shape the component doesn't actually render. As of
this pass, no component in this package authors a genuine second DOM shape (things like a checkbox's
`-label-placement-*` only reorder the same markup via CSS, which isn't a `@variant`), so none carry one.

## Authoring a record

```ts
export const foo = defineComponent({
  name,
  summary,
  modifiers,
  parts,
  cssProperties,
  examples,
  structure,
  demo,
  css: (p) => // prettier-ignore
  css`…css body…`,
});
export const fooCss = foo.css;
```

- The doc comment is **metadata** — plain strings, no backtick/`${` escaping.
- Only the `css` body stays a template literal. **Tag it with `css` and put a `// prettier-ignore`
  line right before it** (before the template for a direct arrow body, before `return` for a block).
  oxfmt treats `css` and `styled` tagged templates as embedded CSS and corrupts interpolated
  selectors (`${p}foo.-mod` → `${p}foo .-mod`, a different meaning) otherwise. Setting
  `embeddedLanguageFormatting` to off does **not** stop it. See the engineering log.
- Add the record to its bucket `index.ts`. For `COMPONENTS` the order is **load-bearing** — it matches
  the `componentsCss()` concat order, not alphabetical.

## Example Audiences

result.content:
## Common recipes

- **Bootstrap a plain web app:** `npm i @pantoken/components` then import `base.css` +
  `components.css` (+ `utilities.css` as needed). Apply classes like `class="instui-button"` to your
  markup. Add `@pantoken/plugin-layouts` for an app-shell layout and
  `@pantoken/plugin-custom-components` for extra components (`card`, `banner`, `agent-shell`).
- **Style from raw tokens only (no components):** `npm i @pantoken/css` then
  `import "@pantoken/css/inject";`. Use `var(--instui-color-background-brand)` etc. in your own CSS.
- **Icons anywhere:** `npm i @pantoken/web-components`, `import "@pantoken/web-components";`, then
  `<instui-icon name="check-mark"></instui-icon>`.
- **Component behaviors (vanilla JS):** `npm i @pantoken/interactions`, then import `initModal`, `initTooltip`, `initInPlaceEdit`, or `initCloseButton` to wire behaviors. For CDN/IIFE: link `@pantoken/interactions/dist/interactions.iife.js` and check `component-capabilities.json` for per-component `.iife.js` entry points.
- **Tailwind:** add `pantokenPreset()` to `presets` and import `@pantoken/css`.
- **Native app:** `npx pantoken generate swift --out ./ios/Tokens --icons arrow-left,check-mark`.
- **Rust app:** `npx pantoken generate rust --out ./src/tokens.rs --format egui`.
- **Sendable email:** use `inlineEmailHtml(html, { client: "generic" })` from `@pantoken/email`, or
  `pantoken generate email`; use `emailTokens()` only when interpolating individual token values.
- **Push to Figma:** `toFigmaVariables(tokens)` → feed a Figma plugin / the Variables REST API.

# Understanding [SC 2.5.3](https://w3.org/TR/WCAG22#label-in-name) Label in Name (Level A)

## In Brief

Goal

The visual label for controls is a trigger for speech activation.

What to do

Where practical, make the control’s text label and name match.

Why it's important

People who operate with voice interaction use the visible labels in their commands.

## Success Criterion (SC)

For [user interface components](#dfn-user-interface-component) with [labels](#dfn-label) that include [text](#dfn-text) or [images of text](#dfn-image-of-text), the [name](#dfn-name) contains the text that is presented visually.

Note

A best practice is to have the text of the label at the start of the name.

## Intent

The intent of this success criterion is to ensure that the words which visually label a component are also the words associated with the component programmatically. This helps ensure that people with disabilities can rely on visible labels as a means to interact with the components.

Most controls are accompanied by a visible text **label**. Those same controls have a programmatic **name**, also known as the [accessible name](https://www.w3.org/TR/accname/#dfn-accessible-name). Users typically have a much better experience if the words and characters in the visible label of a control match or are contained within the accessible name. When these match, speech-input users (i.e., users of speech recognition applications) can navigate by speaking the visible text labels of components, such as menus, links, and buttons, that appear on the screen. Sighted users who use text-to-speech (e.g., screen readers) will also have a better experience if the text they hear matches the text they see on the screen.

Note that where a visible text label does not exist for a component, this success criterion does not apply to that component.

Where text labels exist and are properly linked to the user interface components through established authoring practices, the label and name will normally match. When they don't match, speech-input users who attempt to use the visible text label as a means of navigation or selection (e.g., "move to Password") will be unsuccessful. The speech-based navigation fails because the visible label spoken by the users does not match (or is not part of) the accessible name that is enabled as a speech-input command. In addition, when the accessible name is different from the visible label, it may function as a hidden command that can be accidentally activated by speech-input users.

Mismatches between visible labels and programmatic names for controls are even more of an issue for speech-input and text-to-speech users who also have cognitive challenges. Mismatches create an extra cognitive load for speech-input users, who must remember to say a speech command that is different from the visible label they see on a control. It also creates extra cognitive load for a text-to-speech user to absorb and understand speech output that does not match the visible label.

Note that when a [user interface component](#dfn-user-interface-component) lacks an [accessible name](https://www.w3.org/TR/accname/#dfn-accessible-name) — a failure of [4.1.2 Name, Role, Value](name-role-value) — and has a visible text label, then it also fails this success criterion.

### Identifying label text for components

In order for the label text and accessible name to be matched, it is first necessary to determine which text on the screen should be considered a label for any given control. There are often multiple text strings in a user interface that may be relevant to a control. However, there are reasons why it is best to conservatively interpret the label as being only the text in close proximity.

Conventionally the label for user interface components is the adjacent text string. The typical positioning for left to right languages is:

*   immediately to the left of comboboxes, dropdown lists, text inputs, and other widgets (or in the absence of left-side labels, immediately above and aligned with the left edge of each input)
*   immediately to the right of checkboxes and radio buttons
*   inside buttons and tabs or immediately below icons serving as buttons

The rationale for some of these conventions is explained in [G162: Positioning labels to maximize predictability of relationships](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/general/G162).

It is important to bias towards treating only the adjacent text as a label because liberal interpretations of what constitutes a text label can jeopardize the value of this success criterion (SC) by lessening predictability. Isolating the label to the single string in close proximity to the component makes it easier for developers, testers, and end users to identify the label targeted for evaluation in this SC. Contents of https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/treeview/:
# Tree View Pattern

Tree View Pattern

## About This Pattern

A tree view widget presents a hierarchical list. Any item in the hierarchy may have child items, and items that have children may be expanded or collapsed to show or hide the children. For example, in a file system navigator that uses a tree view to display folders and files, an item representing a folder can be expanded to reveal the contents of the folder, which may be files, folders, or both. 

When using a keyboard to navigate a tree, a visual keyboard indicator informs the user which item is focused. If the tree allows the user to choose just one item for an action, then it is known as a single-select tree. In some implementations of single-select tree, the focused item also has a selected state; this is known as selection follows focus. However, in multi-select trees, which enable the user to select more than one item for an action, the selected state is always independent of the focus. For example, in a typical file system navigator, the user can move focus to select any number of files for an action, such as copy or move. It is important that the visual design distinguish between items that are selected and the item that has focus. For more details, see [this description of differences between focus and selection](../../practices/keyboard-interface/#kbd_focus_vs_selection) and [Deciding When to Make Selection Automatically Follow Focus](../../practices/keyboard-interface/#kbd_selection_follows_focus). 

![](../../../../content-images/wai-aria-practices/images/pattern-treeview.svg)

## Examples

*   [File Directory Treeview Example Using Computed Properties](examples/treeview-1a/): A file selector tree that demonstrates browser support for automatically computing `aria-level`, `aria-posinset` and `aria-setsize` based on DOM structure.
*   [File Directory Treeview Example Using Declared Properties](examples/treeview-1b/): A file selector tree that demonstrates how to explicitly define values for `aria-level`, `aria-posinset` and `aria-setsize`.
*   [Navigation Treeview Example](examples/treeview-navigation/): A tree that provides navigation to a set of web pages and demonstrates browser support for automatically computing `aria-level`, `aria-posinset` and `aria-setsize` based on DOM structure.

## Terms

Terms for describing tree views include:

Node

An item in a tree.

Root Node

Node at the base of the tree; it may have one or more child nodes but does not have a parent node.

Child Node

Node that has a parent; any node that is not a root node is a child node.

End Node

Node that does not have any child nodes; an end node may be either a root node or a child node.

Parent Node

Node with one or more child nodes. It can be open (expanded) or closed (collapsed). 

Open Node

Parent node that is expanded so its child nodes are visible.

Closed Node

Parent node that is collapsed so the child nodes are not visible.

## Keyboard Interaction

For a vertically oriented tree:

*   When a single-select tree receives focus:
    *   If none of the nodes are selected before the tree receives focus, focus is set on the first node.
    *   If a node is selected before the tree receives focus, focus is set on the selected node.
*   When a multi-select tree receives focus:
    *   If none of the nodes are selected before the tree receives focus, focus is set on the first node.
    *   If one or more nodes are selected before the tree receives focus, focus is set on the first selected node.
*   Right arrow:
    *   When focus is on a closed node, opens the node; focus does not move.
    *   When focus is on a open node, moves focus to the first child node.
    *   When focus is on an end node, does nothing.
*   Left arrow:
    *   When focus is on an open node, closes the node.
    *   When focus is on a child node that is also either an end node or a closed node, moves focus to its parent node.
    *   When focus is on a root node that is also either an end node or a closed node, does nothing.
*   Down Arrow: Moves focus to the next node that is focusable without opening or closing a node.
*   Up Arrow: Moves focus to the previous node that is focusable without opening or closing a node.
*   Home: Moves focus to the first node in the tree without opening or closing a node.
*   End: Moves focus to the last node in the tree that is focusable without opening a node.
*   Enter: activates a node, i.e., performs its default action. For parent nodes, one possible default action is to open or close the node. In single-select trees where selection does not follow focus (see note below), the default action is typically to select the focused node.
*   Type-ahead is recommended for all trees, especially for trees with more than 7 root nodes:
    *   Type a character: focus moves to the next node with a name that starts with the typed character.
    *   Type multiple characters in rapid succession: f

# Navigation Treeview Example

Navigation Treeview Example

The code in this example is not intended for production environments. Before using it for any purpose, read this to understand why. 

This is an illustrative example of one way of using ARIA that conforms with the ARIA specification.

*   There may be support gaps in some [browser and assistive technology combinations](../../../../practices/read-me-first/#browser_and_AT_support), especially for [mobile/touch devices](../../../../practices/read-me-first/#mobile_and_touch_support). Testing code based on this example with assistive technologies is essential before considering use in production systems.
*   The [ARIA and Assistive Technologies Project](https://aria-at.w3.org) is developing measurements of assistive technology support for APG examples.
*   Robust accessibility can be further optimized by choosing implementation patterns that [maximize use of semantic HTML](https://www.w3.org/TR/using-aria/#rule1) and heeding the warning that [No ARIA is better than Bad ARIA](../../../../practices/read-me-first/#no_aria_better_bad_aria).

## About This Example

### Caution!

Before considering use of the [Tree View Pattern](../../) for site navigation, it is important to understand:

*   Correct implementation of the `tree` role requires implementation of complex functionality that is not needed for typical site navigation that is styled to look like a tree with expandable sections.
*   A pattern more suited for typical site navigation with expandable groups of links is the [disclosure pattern.](../../../disclosure/)

![](../../../../../../content-images/wai-aria-practices/images/pattern-treeview.svg)

The below example demonstrates how the [Tree View Pattern](../../) can be used to build a navigation tree for a set of hierarchically organized web pages. It illustrates navigation of a mythical university web site that is comparable to the navigation illustrated in the [Example Disclosure Navigation Menu](../../../disclosure/examples/disclosure-navigation/). As noted above, the disclosure pattern is better suited for most web sites because few sites need the additional keyboard functionality required to support the ARIA `tree` role. 

This example relies on the browser to compute values for `aria-setsize`, `aria-posinset`, and `aria-level`. The ARIA specification for these properties states that browsers can, but are not required to, compute their values. So, some browser and assistive technology combinations may not compute or report correct position and level information if it is not explicitly declared. If testing reveals gaps in support for these properties, override automatic computation by explicitly declaring their values as demonstrated in the example of a [File Directory Treeview Example Using Declared Properties.](../treeview-1b/) 

Similar examples include:

*   [File Directory Treeview using _computed_ properties](../treeview-1a/)
*   [File Directory Treeview using _declared_ properties](../treeview-1b/)

result.content:
### Identifying label text for components

In order for the label text and accessible name to be matched, it is first necessary to determine which text on the screen should be considered a label for any given control. There are often multiple text strings in a user interface that may be relevant to a control. However, there are reasons why it is best to conservatively interpret the label as being only the text in close proximity.

Conventionally the label for user interface components is the adjacent text string. The typical positioning for left to right languages is:

*   immediately to the left of comboboxes, dropdown lists, text inputs, and other widgets (or in the absence of left-side labels, immediately above and aligned with the left edge of each input)
*   immediately to the right of checkboxes and radio buttons
*   inside buttons and tabs or immediately below icons serving as buttons

The rationale for some of these conventions is explained in [G162: Positioning labels to maximize predictability of relationships](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/general/G162).

It is important to bias towards treating only the adjacent text as a label because liberal interpretations of what constitutes a text label can jeopardize the value of this success criterion (SC) by lessening predictability. Isolating the label to the single string in close proximity to the component makes it easier for developers, testers, and end users to identify the label targeted for evaluation in this SC. Predictable interpretation of labeling allows users of speech recognition technologies to interact with the element via its conventionally positioned label, and allows users of screen reading technologies to enjoy consistency between the nearby visible label and the announced name of the component.

Note that placeholder text within an input field is not considered an appropriate means of providing a label. The [HTML Standard](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/input.html#the-placeholder-attribute) states The placeholder attribute should not be used as an alternative to a `label`. However, it is worth noting that "label" in that statement is in code brackets and links to the `label` element. For the purposes of this Label in Name Success Criterion, "label" is not used in such a programmatic sense but is simply referring to a text string in close visual proximity to a component. As such, in the absence of any other nearby text string (as described in the preceding list), if an input contains placeholder text, such text may be a candidate for Label in Name. This is supported both through the accessible name calculation (discussed later) and from the practical sense that where a visible label is not otherwise provided, it is likely that a speech-input user may attempt to use the placeholder text value as a means of interacting with the input.

data.content:
# Agent Customization

## Decision Flow

| Primitive | When to Use |
|-----------|-------------|
| agent instructions | Always-on, applies everywhere in the project |
| File Instructions | Explicit via `applyTo` patterns, or on-demand via `description` |
| MCP | Integrates external systems, APIs, or data |
| Hooks | Deterministic shell commands at agent lifecycle points (block tools, auto-format, inject context) |
| Custom Agents | Subagents for context isolation, or multi-stage workflows with tool restrictions |
| Prompts | Single focused task with parameterized inputs |
| Skills | On-demand workflow with bundled assets (scripts/templates) |

## Quick Reference

Consult the reference docs for templates, domain examples, advanced frontmatter options, asset organization, anti-patterns, and creation checklists. If the references are not enough, load the official documentation links for each primitive.

| Type | File | Location | Reference |
|------|------|----------|-----------|
| agent instructions | `copilot-instructions.md`, `AGENTS.md` | `.github/` or root | [Link](./references/agent-instructions.md) |
| File Instructions | `*.instructions.md` | `.github/instructions/` | [Link](./references/instructions.md) |
| Prompts | `*.prompt.md` | `.github/prompts/` | [Link](./references/prompts.md) |
| Hooks | `*.json` | `.github/hooks/` | [Link](./references/hooks.md) |
| Custom Agents | `*.agent.md` | `.github/agents/` | [Link](./references/agents.md) |
| Skills | `SKILL.md` | `.github/skills/<name>/`, `.agents/skills/<name>/`, `.claude/skills/<name>/` | [Link](./references/skills.md) |

**User-level**: `{{VSCODE_USER_PROMPTS_FOLDER}}/` (*.prompt.md, *.instructions.md, *.agent.md; not skills)
Customizations roam with user's settings sync

## Creation Process

If you need to explore or validate patterns in the codebase, use a read-only subagent. If the ask-questions tool is available, use it to interview the user and clarify requirements.

Follow these steps when creating any customization file.

### 1. Determine Scope

Ask the user where they want the customization:
- **Workspace**: For project-specific, team-shared customizations → `.github/` folder
- **User profile**: For personal, cross-workspace customizations → `{{VSCODE_USER_PROMPTS_FOLDER}}/`

### 2. Choose the Right Primitive

Use the Decision Flow above to select the appropriate file type based on the user's need.

### 3. Create the File

Create the file directly at the appropriate path:
- Use the location tables in each reference file
- Include required frontmatter as needed
- Add the body content following the templates

### 4. Validate

After creating:
- Confirm the file is in the correct location
- Verify frontmatter syntax (YAML between `---` markers)
- Check that `description` is present and meaningful

## Edge Cases

**Instructions vs Skill?** Does this apply to *most* work, or *specific* tasks? Most → Instructions. Specific → Skill.

**Skill vs Prompt?** Both appear as slash commands in chat (type `/`). Multi-step workflow with bundled assets → Skill. Single focused task with inputs → Prompt.

**Skill vs Custom Agent?** Same capabilities for all steps → Skill. Need context isolation (subagent returns single output) or different tool restrictions per stage → Custom Agent.

**Hooks vs Instructions?** Instructions *guide* agent behavior (non-deterministic). Hooks *enforce* behavior via shell commands at lifecycle events like `PreToolUse` or `PostToolUse` — they can block operations, require approval, or run formatters deterministically. Hooks can be defined in standalone `.json` files (see [hooks reference](./references/hooks.md)) or inline in custom agent frontmatter via the `hooks` attribute (see [agents reference](./references/agents.md)).

## Common Pitfalls

**Description is the discovery surface.** The `description` field is how the agent decides whether to load a skill, instruction, or agent. If trigger phrases aren't IN the description, the agent won't find it. Use the "Use when..." pattern with specific keywords.

**YAML frontmatter silent failures.** Unescaped colons in values, tabs instead of spaces, `name` that doesn't match folder name — all cause silent failures with no error message. Always quote descriptions that contain colons: `description: "Use when: doing X"`.

**`applyTo: "**"` burns context.** This means "always included for every file request" — it loads the instruction into the context window on every interaction, even when irrelevant. Use specific globs (`**/*.py`, `src/api/**`) unless the instruction truly applies to all files.
data.description: **WORKFLOW SKILL** — Create, update, review, fix, or debug VS Code agent customization files (.instructions.md, .prompt.md, .agent.md, SKILL.md, copilot-instructions.md, AGENTS.md). USE FOR: saving coding preferences; troubleshooting why instructions/skills/agents are ignored or not invoked; configuring applyTo patterns; defining tool restrictions; creating custom agent modes or specialized workflows; packaging domain knowledge; fixing YAML frontmatter syntax. DO NOT USE FOR: general coding questions (use default agent); runtime debugging or error diagnosis; MCP server configuration (use MCP docs directly); VS Code extension development. INVOKES: file system tools (read/write customization files), ask-questions tool (interview user for requirements), subagents for codebase exploration. FOR SINGLE OPERATIONS: For quick YAML frontmatter fixes or creating a single file from a known pattern, edit the file directly — no skill needed.

**Considering testing integration**

I’m analyzing whether we need to add committed integration browser tests. Currently, one-off verifications aren't persistent, and we need to ensure code coverage with robust tests for user interactions and web components. I should add lifecycle tests, focusing on scenarios involving the runtime tree branch and behaviors of disabled nodes. I’m also concerned about how selecting disabled elements impacts functionality and whether we should clarify supporting multi-select functionality since it's unsupported. I want to ensure consumers have clear guidelines!

**Evaluating selection types**

I’m considering the user’s feedback on the InstUI single selection type. It seems effective because it ensures that each DOM gets its own parent IDs, and there are no dynamic event modifications documented for reinitialization. In nested trees, it looks like the selected parent events won't be called since it owns the selection and is set to false. I need to ensure that this behavior continues to work as expected and provides a good user experience.

# pantoken rules (Instructure design tokens & icons)

- Use pantoken tokens: CSS custom properties `--instui-<group>-<name>`. Prefer `var(--instui-*)`
  references over hard-coded values so light/dark and high-contrast theming works. Resolve names
  from `@pantoken/tokens`; do not invent them.
- Route maintained apps to package-manager integration. Route a single HTML mockup or sendable email
  to the `create-pantoken-mockup` skill instead of scaffolding a project.
- In shadcn projects, use `shadcn search/view/add @pantoken/...` for CSS styles and metadata. The
  registry does not provide React components; `@pantoken/shadcn` is the variable bridge.
- Web: `import "@pantoken/css/inject";`. Icons: `@pantoken/web-components` (`<instui-icon>`).
- React: `@pantoken/react`. Tailwind: `@pantoken/tailwind` preset.
- Native / other ecosystems: `npx pantoken generate <swift|android|compose|flutter|rust|wordpress|vanilla|drupal|jekyll|hugo> --out <dir>`.
- Check the [target compatibility registry](https://pantoken.app/target-compatibility.json) before recommending a host version; the
  registry's `$schema` field links its schema. Only named versions or environments are verified.
- InstUI React components: `@instructure/ui-*`. pantoken is the token/icon layer.

---
name: init-pantoken
description: Install pantoken's agent assets (AGENTS.md, llms.txt, editor/agent rule files, and app/mockup skills) into this repo so AI tools know how to work with pantoken. Use when the user asks to add pantoken AI support, or wants Copilot/Cursor/Windsurf/Claude rules for pantoken set up in a repo.
---

# Init pantoken (AI assets)

Install pantoken's consumer-facing agent assets into the current repo: `AGENTS.md`, `llms.txt`,
editor/agent rule files (Cursor, Copilot, Windsurf), and the `create-pantoken-app`,
`create-pantoken-mockup`, and `use-pantoken-registry` skills.

```sh
npx pantoken-ai init
```

This installs every asset by default. To scope it to one tool, pass
`--tool <agents|llms|cursor|copilot|windsurf|claude>`. To target a directory other than the
current one, pass `--dir <path>`. Substitute `pnpm dlx`, `yarn dlx`, `bunx`, or `deno run npm:` for `npx` depending
on the package manager detected in the repo (look for `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `yarn.lock`, or
`bun.lock`/`bun.lockb`; default to npm/npx if none is found).

That's all this skill does — it only writes the asset files above, it does not install any
`@pantoken/*` package or modify application code. Once the assets are installed, use
`create-pantoken-app` for a maintained project (or run `npx pantoken-ai scaffold <platform>`
directly), use `create-pantoken-mockup` for a standalone browser or email artifact, and use
`use-pantoken-registry` when a shadcn project should search, inspect, or add Pantoken registry
items.

**Fixing IIFE queries**

I'm noticing an issue related to the IIFE (immediately-invoked function expression) after loading a combined script. When it queries `.instui-tree-browser[role=tree]`, it now matches a custom host, causing duplicate keyboard events when using arrow keys and toggle clicks firing twice.

Earlier, I thought excluding web hosts that don't have the role of "tree" would help, but since we changed to a host with that role, I need to refine the filter by checking if `el.localName.includes("-")` for custom tags. It's a bit tricky, but I believe I can sort it out!

**Refining custom tree host checks**

I'm considering how to handle registered custom tree hosts more effectively. Using `tree.shadowRoot?.querySelector('[part="tree-browser"]')` can be unreliable since it might not always point to the correct shadow DOM. I should skip any element with a hyphen in its `localName`, as they represent custom elements. It’s reasonable to limit the scope to plain HTML documents and ensure I’m using clear queries to avoid duplicating event handling. 

Additionally, I need a robust solution that checks for both custom elements and their behaviors while preventing multiple initializations. I'll look into using WeakMap for state management to clean things up if they’re called twice.

**Avoiding duplicates in IIFE**

I'm realizing that if the same IIFE script runs twice, it could create a duplicate root, which isn't needed unless it requires a specific scope. To avoid issues with stale data, I could use a data attribute flag alongside a `WeakMap` to prevent duplicates within the same bundle.

I also want to ensure that I’m not introducing risky shortcuts. By documenting auto-skipping for custom tags, I can minimize the chance of duplicates without needing a cleanup API. It’s crucial to test browser behavior with both combined resources and custom elements to ensure everything works smoothly in production!

# Component accessibility remediation plan

Status: step 0 completed in `bd1732042`; step 1 authorized, with semantic decisions pending.
Prepared: 2026-10-27.

## Scope and prerequisites

Remediate findings from the authored `formats/components` audit, preserving the public CSS API
and reusing production behaviors from `@pantoken/interactions`. Include web-component parity
where a shared behavior changes. Don't turn this into a general redesign or an audit of every
renderer.

Planning can proceed while CI runs. Before implementation:

1. Review the hosted CI run for branch `add-automatica11y` (completed successfully):
   https://github.com/thedannywahl/pantoken/actions/runs/40562948018.
   Check the advisory accessibility job and its artifact explicitly; a green required gate alone
   doesn't establish that the advisory audit completed.
2. Obtain and review the actual Snyk scan result for the implementation branch. The CLI's
   availability is not evidence that a scan ran. This remains unverified in this session.
3. Confirm the semantic decisions below one at a time, starting with the tree-browser contract.
4. Preserve the existing audit artifacts as immutable baseline evidence.

The test-concurrency prerequisite is complete: commit `33739d868` caps Vitest at two workers,
and the exact `vp run ready` command passed 179/179 tasks and 3,243 tests. This fixes the
resource-contention problem without increasing timeouts or reducing coverage thresholds.

## Baseline and evidence coverage

Baseline snapshot: 2026-10-27, before remediation, using locally packed packages.
Tool versions from original results: automatica11y 0.11.0, axe-core 4.14.0, IBM checker 4.0.34,
Playwright 1.64.1, Chromium 156.0.8078.48.
Settings: WCAG 2.2 AA, both engines, rebrand/canvas/canvasHighContrast, light/dark.
Library accessibility option: `n/a` for these plain-HTML targets.

| Surface | Cases | Evidence available |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Registered component/member examples and focus declaration | 456 | Rules, conditions, simulated VSR on expanded pages |
| Nine authored npm archetypes | 54 | Rules, interactions, computed, conditions, simulated VSR in initial configuration |
| Additional opened/expanded/message npm configurations | 30 configurations within the 54 targets | Rules and simulated VSR only |

Page and npm evidence are complementary, not equivalent. Page setup opens native surfaces; it
doesn't demonstrate that production activation or keyboard handling works.

Evidence index:
`a11y-report/2026-10-27T17-25-10.017Z-npm-verification/index.md`.
Page originals:
`a11y-report/2026-10-27T16-21-38.658Z/pages-<theme>-<scheme>/{report.md,results.json}`.
Npm originals:
`a11y-report/2026-10-27T17-25-10.017Z-npm-verification/npm-<archetype>/{report.md,results.json}`.
Authored npm fixtures are under the latter run's `fixtures/` directory.

Important correction: all 510 targets completed, but that is not complete per-state tier coverage.
Original `outcome.coverage` arrays contain 90 missing-tier notices: interactions, computed, and
conditions are absent from each of 30 additional configurations for dialog, menu, accordion,
tooltip, and live-region. The current aggregate gap counter doesn't include those notices.
Don't repeat the previous "zero gaps" interpretation.

## Finding inventory

Counts below are result entries across cases/configurations, not unique defects or affected DOM
nodes. Deduplicate root causes before scheduling changes; never add engine counts together.

| Evidence category | Baseline |
| --- | ---: |
| axe-core violations | 26 |
| axe-core incomplete / needs review | 52 |
| IBM Equal Access violations | 74 |
| IBM Equal Access incomplete / needs review | 2,158 |
| Interaction failures | 36 |
| Computed-check failures | 0 |
| Conditions failures | 97 |
| Simulated VSR unnamed-control flags | 6 |
| Additional-configuration missing-tier notices | 90 |

### Rule-engine findings

| Priority | Records | axe-core | IBM Equal Access |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P1 | tree-browser | `aria-required-children` (critical, 6), `listitem` (serious, 6) | `aria_child_tabbable` (Toolkit 1, 6), `aria_widget_labelled` (Toolkit 1, 6) |
| P1 | number-input | `aria-hidden-focus` (serious, 6) | `aria_hidden_nontabbable` (Toolkit 2, 6) |
| P1 | menu, menu.item, menu.separator; npm menu | `color-contrast` (serious, 8) | `text_contrast_sufficient` (Toolkit 1, 8) |
| P2 | drawer-layout and members | None reported as violations | `aria_role_valid` (Toolkit 1, 12), `aria_complementary_labelled` (Toolkit 3, 6), `aria_region_labelled` (Toolkit 3, 18) |
| P2 | radio-input-group | None reported as violations | `fieldset_label_valid` (Toolkit 3, 6), `input_checkboxes_grouped` (Toolkit 2, 6) |

Menu contrast findings are concentrated in canvas and canvasHighContrast dark cases. IBM reports
2.36:1 for 16px, weight-400 text; verify the exact resolved foreground, actual painted backdrop,
and rest/hover/focus/selected state before choosing a fix. Don't alter upstream tokens merely to
silence a local cascade problem.

### Interactions

Each check below fails in six theme/scheme targets:

- Modal: `focus-moves-into-dialog`, `escape-closes`.
- Menu: `arrow-keys-move-between-items`.
- Form field: `error-associated-on-invalid`.
- Tooltip: `escape-dismisses`, `content-reachable-on-hover`.

### Conditions and simulated screen-reader output

- Reflow at 320 CSS pixels: 64 failures involving pill, drawer layout/members, tooltip, and
  table/members. Judge legitimate two-dimensional table exceptions manually; don't blanket-waive
  all tables or mask overflow globally.
- Reduced motion: 24 failures involving spinner, toggle-details, and mask.
- Text spacing: six avatar failures; name parts are clipped under the tool's spacing settings.
- Reduced transparency: three failures involving tag and number-input. The tool explicitly says
  this preference is not a WCAG requirement; track it as a separate user-preference enhancement.
- Simulated VSR: six checkbox unnamed-control flags. Compare the actual accessibility tree and
  authored label association before deciding whether this is markup or simulator behavior.

# Authoring `@pantoken/components`

`@pantoken/components` is the semantic RSCSS CSS API — a parameterized generator, not hand-written
CSS. Each documented record is one file; the bucket `index.ts` is a barrel + registry, not a monolith.

## Source layout

- `src/components/<name>/index.ts` + `<name>.css` (`COMPONENTS` registry).
- `src/components/<name>/members/<member>/index.ts` + `<member>.css` — a promoted sub-component (see
  "Sub-components (`@memberOf`)" below).
- `src/utilities/<name>/index.ts` + `<name>.css` (`UTILITIES`).
- `src/rules/{base,prose}/index.ts` + `<name>.css` (`RULES`).
- `src/declarations/<name>/index.ts` + `<name>.css` (`DECLARATIONS`).
- `src/lib/`: `helpers.ts` (ns/scope/glyph consts/spacing scales/`ComponentOptions`/`DEFAULT_PREFIX`),
  `define.ts` (`defineComponent`/`defineUtility`/`defineRule`/`defineDeclaration`), `aliases.ts`
  (`withSizeAliases`/`withAliases`), `css.ts` (the identity `css` tag), `headings.ts`,
  `field-controls.ts`.

## Sub-components (`@memberOf`)

When a component maps to a real, separately-named instui sub-component export (`Tabs.Panel`,
`Table.Row`, `Menu.Item`, …), promote it to its own record instead of documenting it as a `@part`
bullet on the parent:

- New files: `src/components/<parent>/members/<member>/<member>.css` + `index.ts`, same shape as any
  other record (`defineComponent`, registered in `COMPONENTS`, exported from `src/index.ts`).
- The record's cssdoc name is **dotted**: `@component <parent>.<member>` (e.g. `@component menu.item`)
  — this keeps member names globally unique across the whole registry even when two different parents
  have a same-named part (`menu.item` vs `side-nav-bar.item`), which a bare `item`/`item` collision
  would break for the `providers`-indexed cross-file `@memberOf`/`@structure` resolution. The TS
  identifier stays camelCase (`menuItem`/`menuItemCss`), since a dot isn't legal there anyway.
- Add `@memberOf <parent>` on the member's own record.
- **Always author an explicit `@class .<member>`** (or `@selector`) rather than relying on inference —
  a member's CSS typically keeps the parent's `@scope (.pfx-<parent>) { … }` wrapper (real cascade
  scoping, not just documentation), and inference across that boundary is unreliable; the fallback
  className for a dotted name (`.menu.item`) would also be misleading.
- **Physically move the CSS** into the member's own file — don't leave a doc-only record pointing at
  rules that still live in the parent. The aggregator just concatenates raw CSS text regardless of
  which file it came from, so this is safe even for native-element selectors with no `@scope` (e.g.
  `table.row`'s `tr`) or where a shared declaration has to be duplicated across a couple of sibling
  members (e.g. `table.-layout-stacked`'s box-reset, split per part rather than kept as one
  five-selector compound rule) — cssdoc requires each record's own file to own its own selectors.
- Remove the promoted `@part` line — a `@memberOf` record documents its own structure on its own page,
  and `@memberOf` alone (independent of nesting in the parent's own `@structure`) already feeds the
  parent's generated "Subcomponents" section.
- Give the member's own `@structure` an `@component <parent> { … }` node instead of a bare
  `@scope (.pfx-<parent>) { … }` wrapper — this embeds the member's real ancestor path (down to the
  member's own selector, with any of its own nested parts) as a cross-linked record reference, e.g.
  `@component table { tbody { tr { td {} } } }` for `table.cell`. See the `table.*` members for the
  full pattern, including a sibling-alternation node like `table.body`'s `tbody`.
- If a parent-level modifier restyles a promoted member (e.g. `tabs`'s `-variant-secondary` restyling
  `tabs.tab`, or `table`'s `-layout-stacked` restyling all six of its members), mark it inline:
  `@modifier -variant-secondary — … @affects tabs.tab — …`. Multiple `@affects <parent>.<member>`
  markers can follow one another on the same `@modifier` line.
- Register the member in `COMPONENTS` right after its parent, export `<member>Css` from `src/index.ts`
  next to the parent's export, and add it to `tests/public-surface.test.ts`'s `EXPECTED` list (that
  array is sorted before comparison, so insertion position doesn't matter). Fix any existing test that
  asserted on the parent's `xxxCss` for content that moved to the member.
- Don't promote a `@part` just because it's stylistically distinct — the bar is a **real, separately
  exported instui component** (`List.Item` yes; a passive style hook like byline's `.title`/`.description`
  or tabs' `.list`, which has no corresponding `Tabs.List` export, no).

## Alternate DOM shapes (`@variant`)

`@structure` supports `@variant <name>? { … }` blocks for a component that genuinely renders one of
several alternative DOM shapes (e.g. a `<label>` wrapping a control vs. a `<label for>` plus a sibling
control). Only add one when a second shape is **already real and CSS-supported** — check the record's
existing `@example`s and rules first; don't invent a shape the component doesn't actually render. As of
this pass, no component in this package authors a genuine second DOM shape (things like a checkbox's
`-label-placement-*` only reorder the same markup via CSS, which isn't a `@variant`), so none carry one.

## Authoring a record

```ts
export const foo = defineComponent({
  name,
  summary,
  modifiers,
  parts,
  cssProperties,
  examples,
  structure,
  demo,
  css: (p) => // prettier-ignore
  css`…css body…`,

entire checkpoint explain — Explain a session, commit, or checkpoint
Explain provides human-readable context about sessions, commits, and checkpoints.

Use this command to understand what happened during agent-driven development,
either for self-review or to understand a teammate's work.

By default, shows checkpoints on the current branch. Pass a checkpoint ID or
commit SHA as a positional argument to explain a specific item, or use flags.

Viewing specific items:
  entire checkpoint explain <id-or-sha>           Auto-detects checkpoint ID or commit SHA
  entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <id>     Force interpretation as checkpoint ID
  entire checkpoint explain --commit <ref>        Force interpretation as commit ref

Checkpoints in another repo:
  entire checkpoint explain <id-or-sha> --repo gh/owner/name
  entire checkpoint explain <id-or-sha> --repo et/project/repo
                 Explain a checkpoint owned by another repository — the
                 drill-down for a cross-repo 'entire search' hit. Reads it from
                 that repo's Entire API; nothing is written to this repo.
                 Needs a full checkpoint ID (12-char hex or 26-char ULID) or a full commit SHA
                 (positional, --checkpoint, or --commit) and a checkpoint that
                 has been pushed. A commit SHA is resolved to its checkpoint
                 by that repo's Entire API, so prefixes cannot be used here.

Filtering the list view:
  --session      Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)

Output verbosity levels (when explaining a specific item):
  Default:         Detailed view with scoped prompts (ID, session, tokens, intent, prompts, files)
  --short          Summary only (ID, session, timestamp, tokens, intent)
  --full           Parsed full transcript (all prompts/responses from entire session)
  --raw-transcript Raw transcript file (JSONL format)

Machine-readable export modes (additive surface for external consumers):
  --json           Metadata-only JSON. Lists checkpoints when no target is given;
                   emits a single checkpoint envelope when a target is supplied,
                   including its subagent task records under "tasks".
                   Transcript bytes are NEVER embedded in the JSON envelope.
  --transcript     Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes (JSONL) to stdout
                   for the selected session. Same bytes as --raw-transcript
                   while checkpoints v1 is the checkpoint store.
  --session-index  Pick a session within a multi-session checkpoint (0-based).
                   Defaults to the latest session. Only meaningful with
                   --transcript or --raw-transcript.
  --task           With --transcript, stream a subagent's stored transcript
                   instead, selected by tool_use_id or agent_id (as listed
                   under "tasks" in --json).
  --limit          Cap the number of checkpoints returned by the list view.
                   Defaults to 100. When the cap is hit, a stderr note
                   says how many were skipped. Only meaningful with --json.

Summary generation:
  --generate    Generate an AI summary for the checkpoint. This is the only
                part of this command that writes: it stores the summary on the
                checkpoint and spends tokens with the configured summary
                provider. Every other mode only reads.
  --force       Regenerate even if a summary already exists (requires --generate)

Performance options:
  --search-all  Remove branch/depth limits when searching for commits (may be slow)

Checkpoint detail view shows:
  - Author of the checkpoint
  - Associated git commits that reference the checkpoint
  - Prompts and responses from the session

Note: --session filters the list view; the positional arg, --commit, and --checkpoint are mutually exclusive.

When to use this:
Reading a checkpoint is free: with no flags, or with --json, --full,
--transcript or --raw-transcript, this only reads and is safe to run
whenever you need the context. --generate is the exception — it writes a
summary onto the checkpoint and spends tokens with the summary provider,
so pass it only when the user asked for a summary. To see what subagents
did, read "tasks" in --json, then stream one subagent's transcript with
--transcript --task <tool_use_id>.

Current repo: gh/thedannywahl/pantoken  (auto-detected from origin; pass --repo only for a DIFFERENT repo)

Flags:
  -c, --checkpoint string             Explain a specific checkpoint (ID or prefix)
      --commit string                 Explain a specific commit (SHA or ref, "commit-ish")
      --force                         Regenerate summary even if one already exists (requires --generate)
      --full                          Show full parsed transcript (all prompts/responses)
      --generate                      Generate an AI summary for the checkpoint
      --insecure-http-auth            Allow plain-HTTP auth for --repo (local dev only)
      --json                          Output metadata as JSON (no transcript bytes)
      --limit int                     Cap the list view at N checkpoints (default: 100). Only meaningful with --json.
      --no-pager                      Disable pager output
      --raw-transcript                Show raw transcript file (JSONL format)
      --repo string                   Explain a checkpoint owned by another repo (gh/owner/name, et/project/repo, entire://<host>/gh/<owner>/<repo>, or entire://<host>/et/<project>/<repo>), read from that repo's Entire API
      --search-all                    Search all commits (no branch/depth limit, may be slow)
      --session string                Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)
      --session-index int             Session index within a multi-session checkpoint (0-based, defaults to latest) (default -1)
  -s, --short                         Show summary only (omit prompts and files)
      --summary-timeout-seconds int   Hard deadline in seconds for --generate summary generation; overrides summary_timeout_seconds setting. 0 = use setting; if setting is also unset or 0, no automatic deadline applies.
      --task string                   Subagent task (tool_use_id or agent_id) whose stored transcript --transcript streams
      --transcript                    Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes to stdout (a session's, or a subagent's with --task)

Inherited flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only — including the git and agent processes it spawns — instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

`components.css` (+ `utilities.css` as needed). Apply classes like `class="instui-button"` to your
  markup. Add `@pantoken/plugin-layouts` for an app-shell layout and
  `@pantoken/plugin-custom-components` for extra components (`card`, `banner`, `agent-shell`).
- **Style from raw tokens only (no components):** `npm i @pantoken/css` then
  `import "@pantoken/css/inject";`. Use `var(--instui-color-background-brand)` etc. in your own CSS.
- **Icons anywhere:** `npm i @pantoken/web-components`, `import "@pantoken/web-components";`, then
  `<instui-icon name="check-mark"></instui-icon>`.
- **Component behaviors (vanilla JS):** `npm i @pantoken/interactions`, then import `initModal`, `initTooltip`, `initInPlaceEdit`, or `initCloseButton` to wire behaviors. For CDN/IIFE: link `@pantoken/interactions/dist/interactions.iife.js` and check `component-capabilities.json` for per-component `.iife.js` entry points.
- **Tree browser:** ARIA trees need `initTreeBrowser` or the `tree-browser.iife.js` entry point,
  not CSS alone. Name the tree, use focusable treeitems, and connect collection rows to their groups
  with `aria-owns`. Native details/summary disclosures remain a CSS-only alternative without tree roles.
- **Tailwind:** add `pantokenPreset()` to `presets` and import `@pantoken/css`.
- **Native app:** `npx pantoken generate swift --out ./ios/Tokens --icons arrow-left,check-mark`.
- **Rust app:** `npx pantoken generate rust --out ./src/tokens.rs --format egui`.
- **Sendable email:** use `inlineEmailHtml(html, { client: "generic" })` from `@pantoken/email`, or
  `pantoken generate email`; use `emailTokens()` only when interpolating individual token values.
- **Push to Figma:** `toFigmaVariables(tokens)` → feed a Figma plugin / the Variables REST API.

## The JS-behavior tier

**Addressing build issues**

I'm encountering failures because the dependencies aren't building component styles and scaffold assets properly, leading to outdated copies. I need to explicitly build both components and scaffold earlier in the process. The build command must run `vp run @pantoken/components#build @pantoken/scaffold#build`, which supports multiple selectors. However, there may be some complexity, as tasks could require sequential execution. Additionally, I must ensure tests import the correct components since the current setup is reading old versions. It's all a bit tangled, but I’ll work through it step by step.

**Improving build readability**

I'm thinking about independent work, which is fine, but I need to ensure the readability stage 5 is implemented now. There’s a potential conditional race with the initial build snapshot while build comp reads. I shouldn't make any code edits until the build is complete because that could complicate things. It’s a straightforward process, with form field targets in mind, while I also have to monitor test gating as it's running. I’ll make sure everything runs smoothly!

**Resolving radio label issues**

I’m looking at IBM's radio baseline findings and noticed there's a problem with duplicate legends not using aria-label. It seems the source has no aria labels, which means both fieldsets have identical names that result in an invalid label count. This violates the "More than one legend with the same name" rule. I need to fix this by ensuring unique names for independent groups. Using a toggle size option can help differentiate the groups without duplicating legends. Inspecting the original report might provide more insights without changing legends unnecessarily.

-Next step-1 records: number-input, drawer-layout, radio-input-group, form-field, and investigation
-of checkbox simulated-VSR flags. These and all later stages remain unfinished.
+## Step 1 progress: number-input, drawer-layout, radio groups, and checkbox triage
+
+The user chose to finish step 1 before synchronizing API translations. Publication remains pending;
+the last drift count above predates these additional API documentation changes.
+
+- `e93a997d9` fixes number-input's redundant hidden arrow buttons with `tabindex="-1"` in both
+  documentation and audit examples, matching upstream v2. The native number input retains
+  keyboard ownership. Two test files passed 131 tests. Six audit cases have zero violations in
+  both engines, with five IBM potential/manual reviews per case. Chromium over HTTP verified
+  native Up/Down changes and that Tab skips both arrows in every theme/scheme.
+  Evidence: `a11y-report/2026-10-27T19-44-51.720Z/index.md`.
+- `b6a667fab` fixes drawer-layout and both members. The user chose InstUI-style regions with
+  explicit pane-label attributes. Replaced invalid `main[role=region]` and the unnamed tray
+  wrapper with `div` regions, added reactive `tray-label`/`content-label`, and updated all examples,
+  consumer assets, security docs, and guidance. Applications must provide nonempty pane names;
+  no generic fallback labels are invented. Four test files passed 155 tests; focused runtime
+  coverage is 100% in every metric. All 18 raw HTML cases have zero axe and IBM violations.
+  Chromium verified shadow-region names, dynamic labels, and open/close commands in all six cases.
+  Evidence:
+  - `a11y-report/2026-10-27T19-55-21.577Z/index.md` (root).
+  - `a11y-report/2026-10-27T19-57-11.745Z/index.md` (tray).
+  - `a11y-report/2026-10-27T20-01-18.689Z/index.md` (content).
+- `d7e56cbe8` fixes independent radio groups' duplicated names and legends in documentation and
+  audit examples. Six cases have zero axe and IBM violations. Chromium verified pointer selection,
+  native arrow-key movement, and selection isolation in all six cases.
+  Evidence: `a11y-report/2026-10-27T20-04-32.703Z/index.md`.
+- `a7cfbfb1e` clarifies native checkbox naming and adds label-association regression tests.
+  Investigation found no unnamed checkbox: the original simulated log says
+  `checkbox, Checkbox, checked`, then separately emits the text `Checkbox`. The installed
+  `flagPhrases()` lowercases each phrase and flags any exact role word, so the standalone text
+  triggers its heuristic. Chromium's accessibility tree confirms both native names, `Checkbox`
+  and `Toggle`, in all six original cases. Labels and raw flags remain unchanged; no suppression.
+  Fresh audits still have zero engine violations, five IBM potential reviews per case, and the
+  same six simulator flags. Radio/checkbox plus inventory tests passed 135 tests across three files.
+  Evidence: `a11y-report/2026-10-27T20-07-25.640Z/index.md`.
+
+Each increment includes a Changeset. Related source format, lint/type checks, CSS documentation
+checks, builds, and Markdown checks passed. Test counts overlap; don't sum them.
+
+### Remaining step-1 decision: form-field validation ownership
+
+The audit example contains a required email input but no associated error. Inspection of the
+installed `error-associated-on-invalid` check shows it requires newly associated or newly added
+error text after invalid input; it deliberately doesn't count text linked before interaction.
+Merely adding a static error node won't address that dynamic contract. CSS can reveal a message,
+but can't synchronize ARIA attributes or error references.
+
+No form-field edits have been made. Decide whether to add an opt-in, shared production native
+validation helper with tests and an IIFE entry point, or retain application-owned validation and
+honestly track the dynamic check as unresolved for the CSS-only facade. Don't insert fixture-only
+behavior, remove validation merely to get a not-applicable result, or weaken the check.
+
+Form-field and all later plan stages remain unfinished.

**Evaluating budget and implementation**

I see that there’s a remaining budget of 26k, which seems sufficient, but I have some concerns about token usage being around 50. It's already been an hour, and the user requests keep coming in. I need to think about implementing helper controls and returning functions for validation. It’s essential to define a precise contract before coding to avoid questions later. I'll ensure standard types are allowed, with controls like input, select, or textarea. I’ll implement a validation mechanism that uses `checkValidity`.

**Assessing initial input validity**

I need a valid initial input like `value="[REDACTED_EMAIL]"` in the audit fixture to avoid preflight issues. After the blur event, I want to show errors appropriately while using an arbitrary valid email as an example. If a user deletes the value, it transitions to an error, and the documentation should clarify this behavior. I’m considering how to handle the native invalid event during form submission and ensuring that checkValidity is called correctly without unwanted auto-announcements. The initial field should maintain the valid state for consistency in the future audit tool.

**Re-evaluating event handling for validation**

I’m considering whether to avoid the invalid event listener altogether and rely only on blur and input events for public validation before submission. The native invalid event has browser default requirements and typically only shows errors after a blur event. If the user clicks submit without the field being focused, the helper doesn’t mark an ARIA error, which could lead to accessibility issues. I want to ensure that validation flows through all scenarios and that public validation runs correctly before submission. I'll need to capture invalid events properly on the control.

data.summaryContent:
<overview>
The user wants automatica11y integrated as development tooling for auditing `formats/components`, followed by staged accessibility remediation. They require incremental conventional commits, Changesets, and test coverage; integration, concurrency fixes, coverage accounting, tree-browser, number-input, drawer-layout, radio-group fixes, and checkbox triage are committed. The current uncommitted increment adds an explicitly authorized opt-in native form-validation helper; it has passed unit, production, browser, and initial-state audits, but the latest change to audit visible invalid states still needs verification before committing.
</overview>

<history>
1. **Original integration and process requirements**
   - User: “I want to add automatica11y from npm as a dev tool for auditing the css in formats/components.”
   - User: “work in incremental conventional commits with changesets and test coverage.”
   - Approved local command, advisory CI reporting, explicit authored examples for every registered component/member and focus, rendered pages and npm archetypes, three themes × light/dark, WCAG 2.2 AA, axe-core, and IBM Equal Access.
   - Integration completed in ten commits and audited 456 page targets plus 54 npm targets.

2. **Concurrency, Actions, and Snyk**
   - Explained `gh` dispatches/inspects hosted Actions; local emulation requires `act`, which was unavailable, and Docker’s daemon was stopped.
   - Added shared Vitest `maxWorkers: 2`, a regression test, and docs.
   - Exact `vp run ready` passed 179/179 tasks and 3,243 tests.
   - Committed `33739d868 fix(tooling): bound test workers in readiness runs`.
   - Hosted run **40562948018** on `thedannywahl/pantoken` completed successfully, but it predates current remediation changes.
   - Snyk CLI is installed, but **no source scan has run in this session**. Standard Snyk Code uploads source, and no permitted local/on-prem endpoint is configured. Don’t claim security verification passed.

3. **Remediation plan and step 0**
   - User requested the remediation plan while CI ran.
   - Plan saved and registered at:
     `/Users/dwahl/.copilot/session-state/9347a925-530d-4721-9964-9f9d5f3aa58a/files/accessibility-remediation-plan.md`
   - Found that completing all 510 targets did not imply full per-state coverage: original npm reports contained **90 missing-tier notices**.
   - User: “start with 0, and let me know when it's done, then move one.”
   - Implemented and committed **`bd1732042 fix(components): account for per-state accessibility coverage`**.
   - Corrected baseline: 510 completed targets, 540 configurations, 90 notices; original evidence unchanged.
   - Focused tests passed; runner coverage exceeded thresholds.
   - Told user step 0 was complete and began step 1.

4. **Tree-browser contract and investigation**
   - Asked whether to keep native disclosure navigation or implement a real ARIA tree.
   - User chose whichever most closely aligns with Instructure UI and linked upstream TreeBrowser v2.
   - Inspected upstream: real treeitems, roving tabindex, arrows, j/k, Home/End, RTL-aware expansion, Enter/Space activation, optional single selection, none by default.
   - Added shared Node-free tree behavior, production IIFE, exports, capability metadata, audit loading, web-component lifecycle, examples, and consumer guidance.
   - Expanded nested tree markup exposed `label-content-name-mismatch`.
   - User chose **investigate-first**, not suppression.
   - Minimal Chromium reproduction traced axe’s recursive visible-text comparison. W3C’s navigation-tree example explicitly supports sibling groups owned through `aria-owns`; Chromium exposed equivalent accessibility hierarchy.
   - Adopted that structure without disabling rules or editing results.
   - Committed **`c0e17d87b fix(components): align tree browser accessibility with InstUI`**.
   - Final expanded six-case audit: zero axe and IBM violations, five IBM potential/manual reviews per case.
   - Tests/builds/browser checks passed; tree behavior coverage was 97.29% statements, 92.7% branches, 100% functions/lines.
   - Publication gate failed solely on **516 translation-drift entries across five API pages and 43 locales**.

5. **Translation timing**
   - Asked whether to pause for translation synchronization or finish step 1 first.
   - User explicitly chose **continue-step-one**, deferring translation synchronization.
   - Don’t waive translation policies, copy English into translated fields, or claim publication readiness.
   - The last 516 count predates subsequent documentation changes, so don’t present it as a freshly measured current total.

6. **Number-input**
   - Verified upstream v2 uses both `aria-hidden` and `tabIndex={-1}` for redundant pointer arrow controls.
   - Added `tabindex="-1"` to both arrow buttons in documentation and audit examples.
   - Clarified native input keyboard ownership and consumer responsibility for pointer wiring/focus preservation.
   - Added tests for every authored example.
   - 131 tests passed; six audits had zero violations in both engines.
   - Chromium verified Up/Down changes and that Tab skips arrows in all six theme/scheme cases.
   - Committed **`e93a997d9 fix(components): remove hidden number arrows from tab order`**.

7. **Drawer-layout semantic decision**
   - Found invalid `<main role="region">`, unnamed tray/content landmarks, and no way to name shadow regions.
   - Verified InstUI uses a `<div role="region">` with an author-supplied label; inline tray also uses a region.
   - User explicitly chose **instui-named-regions** rather than neutral wrappers.
   - Replaced pane elements with `div` regions and added reactive `tray-label` and `content-label`.
   - Applications must supply nonempty names; no generic fallback labels are invented.
   - Corrected root/member examples, consumer assets, security docs, and guidance.
   - 155 tests passed; focused runtime coverage was 100% in every metric.
   - All 18 root/member page cases had zero axe/IBM violations.
   - Chromium verified names, updates, and open/close commands across six cases.
   - Committed **`b6a667fab fix(components): name drawer layout regions`**.

8. **Radio groups and checkbox triage**
   - Original radio report explicitly flagged duplicate legends and shared native names across independent fieldsets.
   - Gave plain/toggle groups distinct legends (“T-shirt size” / “Sweatshirt size”) and names (`shirt-size` / `sweatshirt-size`).
   - Added selection-isolation tests; six audits had zero engine violations.
   - Chromium verified clicking visible labels, native arrow movement, and independent selection.
   - Committed **`d7e56cbe8 fix(components): isolate radio group example selections`**.
   - Checkbox investigation showed a simulator heuristic, not missing native names:
     ```
     checkbox, Checkbox, checked
     Checkbox
     checkbox, Toggle, not checked
     Toggle
     ```
   - Installed `flagPhrases()` lowercases each phrase and flags exact role words, so standalone text “Checkbox” is flagged.
   - Chromium accessibility tree confirmed both native names in all six original cases.
   - Kept labels and raw flags unchanged; clarified naming and added tests.
   - Committed **`a7cfbfb1e test(components): verify native checkbox label associations`**.
   - Combined radio/checkbox/inventory run: 135 tests passed.
   - Fresh checkbox audits retained exactly six original-style heuristic flags and zero engine violations.

9. **Form-field validation ownership**
   - Bare audit fixture had required email validation but no associated error.
   - Read the installed dynamic checker: it specifically requires **newly associated or newly added** error text after invalid input; static prelinked text does not count.
   - CSS can reveal text but can’t synchronize ARIA associations.
   - Offered an opt-in production helper versus retaining application-owned validation and honestly tracking the failure.
   - User explicitly chose **opt-in-production-helper**.
   - Implemented shared `initFormField`, production IIFE, build/export/generation wiring, capability metadata, authored examples, tests, consumer guidance, security docs, and Changeset.
   - Unit helper suite: **13 tests, 100% coverage in all metrics**.
   - Final broader validation before the latest fixture change: **300 tests across 21 files passed**; combined runner/helper coverage 96.31% statements, 92.17% branches, 100% functions, 96.35% lines.
   - Production builds, targeted formatting/lint/type checks, CSS documentation checks, and Markdown checks passed.
   - Real six-page + six-npm audit completed successfully, zero engine violations; need explicitly extract/assert the dynamic check outcomes rather than infer them from advisory exit code.
   - Chromium verified visible error associations and actual accessibility descriptions, correction, `hidden` precedence, no-marker behavior, native submission, and reset.
   - **Most recent change, not yet tested:** page fixture setup now uses native validation to reveal required form-field errors, so page rules/conditions/VSR inspect the visible invalid state while npm fixtures retain valid initial state and test the transition. This was added to avoid claiming full coverage from initial-state-only audits. It needs a fresh page audit, tests, and browser helper updates.
</history>

## Form helper contract

```ts
type FormFieldControl =
  HTMLInputElement | HTMLSelectElement | HTMLTextAreaElement;

interface FormFieldHandle {
  validate(): boolean;
  cleanup(): void;
}

initFormField(
  host: HTMLElement,
  control: FormFieldControl,
  error: HTMLElement
): FormFieldHandle;
```

Behavior:
- Requires host containment of control/error, error separate from control, nonempty whitespace-free error ID, and nonempty message text.
- Uses native `willValidate` and `validity.valid`; supports consumer `setCustomValidity()`.
- Starts pristine unless initially `-invalid` or `aria-invalid="true"`.
- Blur, native `invalid`, or explicit `validate()` marks touched and renders validation.
- Input revalidates only after touch.
- Preserves hint IDs, adds/removes only the error ID from `aria-describedby`, deduplicates IDs.
- Sets `aria-invalid`, toggles host `-invalid`, and synchronizes `error.hidden`.
- Doesn’t choose validation policy or message text, parse HTML, move focus, change values, or cancel browser validation.
- Form reset queues pristine-state rendering after native values reset; honors canceled reset and cleanup before queued work.
- Cleanup is idempotent and restores original ARIA attributes, invalid class, and error visibility.
- Calling `validate()` after cleanup throws.
- IDs must stay unique/stable; reinitialize after moving to another form/changing IDs.
- Client-side validation is not server-side validation/security.

Production auto-init:
- Only `.instui-form-field[data-native-validation]`.
- Skips custom-element hosts.
- Exactly one native control and one error message with `-type-error` or `-type-new-error`; malformed markup throws.

# Component accessibility remediation plan

Status: step 0 completed in `bd1732042`; step 1 in progress, with tree-browser committed in `c0e17d87b`.
Prepared: 2026-10-27.

## Step 1 progress: tree-browser

- Followed the user's Instructure UI preference: full ARIA-tree keyboard navigation, not
  disclosure navigation with tree roles removed.
- Added shared Node-free behavior, IIFE initialization, capability metadata, and web-component
  lifecycle delegation. Updated consumer AI assets and security documentation.
- Investigated the expanded-tree label mismatch before proceeding. A minimal Chromium
  reproduction isolated descendant text included by axe's label-content-name-mismatch check.
  Adopted the W3C navigation-tree example's owned sibling groups; Chromium preserves the
  expected accessibility hierarchy. No rule was disabled or result edited.
- Final audit: `node formats/components/scripts/audit-accessibility.ts --record tree-browser`.
  All six theme/scheme cases completed with zero axe violations and zero IBM violations.
  Five IBM potential/manual-review entries remain per case.
  Evidence: `a11y-report/2026-10-27T19-39-40.197Z/index.md`.
- Page fixtures now activate production tree behavior to expand every collection. Chromium
  verified actual expanded states, one tab stop, and no page runtime errors in all six cases.
  Earlier HTTP checks also covered keyboard handling, slotted web components, accessibility
  hierarchy, and CSS-IIFE/custom-element coexistence.
- Validation: 211 focused tests and a 296-test interactions/web-components regression run
  passed (overlapping suites, not additive totals). The final five-file run after audit-setup
  and security-doc changes passed 83 tests. Tree behavior coverage: statements 97.29%,
  branches 92.7%, functions 100%, lines 100%. Production builds, targeted formatting,
  lint/type checks, CSS documentation checks, and related Markdown lint passed.
- Release metadata: `.changeset/twelve-bats-refuse.md` includes components, interactions,
  web-components, scaffold, and AI. Commit: `c0e17d87b`.
- Publication remains blocked: `vp run check:publish` reported 516 translation-drift entries
  across five generated API pages and 43 locales. Don't waive the translation policy or copy
  English into translated fields. Translation synchronization is still required before merge.
- Snyk remains unverified: the installed CLI's standard source scan uploads source, and no
  permitted local/on-prem scanning endpoint is configured.

## Step 1 progress: number-input, drawer-layout, radio groups, and checkbox triage

The user chose to finish step 1 before synchronizing API translations. Publication remains pending;
the last drift count above predates these additional API documentation changes.

- `e93a997d9` fixes number-input's redundant hidden arrow buttons with `tabindex="-1"` in both
  documentation and audit examples, matching upstream v2. The native number input retains
  keyboard ownership. Two test files passed 131 tests. Six audit cases have zero violations in
